en.title: Early Childhood Education: the whole course
en.short: What early childhood education covers, how the course is organised, its main areas and how to study it.

sections.heading: What the subject is
sections.text:
Early Childhood Education (ECE) is the study and practice of educating and caring for young children, usually from birth to about eight years. The age range differs by country: some systems count birth to five, others to eight or the early primary years. The field covers development, play, health, nutrition, safety, language, early mathematics and science, creativity, social and emotional learning, inclusion, child protection, families and policy.

It is not only preparation for school and not babysitting. Young children learn through relationships, play, routine and exploration. Practice starts from the child’s safety, dignity and rights and works with families. Settings include crèches, nurseries, kindergartens, pre-primary and reception classes, and home-based care.

sections.heading: How the course is usually organised
sections.text:
In Nigeria, a Bachelor of Education (B.Ed) in Early Childhood Education is commonly a four-year full-time university programme. Colleges of Education offer the Nigeria Certificate in Education (NCE), commonly over three years. Some institutions also offer diplomas, postgraduate diplomas and master’s degrees. The National Universities Commission (NUC) regulates university programmes and the National Commission for Colleges of Education (NCCE) regulates colleges of education. Titles and durations vary, so check your own handbook.

In Ghana, a Bachelor of Education in Early Childhood Education is commonly four years. In South Africa, the B.Ed Foundation Phase is a four-year initial teacher qualification for Grades R to 3. Other countries use different awards, including diplomas and associate degrees. Programmes usually combine lectures, tutorials, assignments, teaching practice and a final project. Master’s study adds theory, policy and research methods.

sections.heading: Main areas in teaching order
sections.text:
Most courses begin with introductory topics: what ECE is; child growth and development; learning theories for young children; play and play-based learning; observation, assessment and record keeping; health, nutrition and safety; families, communities and culture; language development and emergent literacy; and early mathematics and science foundations.

The core moves to practice: curriculum planning and environment design; language, literacy and multilingual pedagogy; early mathematics pedagogy; early science and inquiry pedagogy; social and emotional learning and guidance; creative arts, music and movement; physical development and outdoor learning; inclusive practice and disability; child protection and safeguarding; infant and toddler care; child assessment and school readiness; digital technology; policy and governance; leadership and management; professional ethics; reflective practice and action research; and teaching practice.

Master’s level is more critical and research based: critical perspectives, research methods, quality and evaluation, and comparative and international policy.

sections.heading: How to study it
sections.text:
Read with a notebook and link theory to a real child or setting you have seen. For each theorist, learn the name, the main claim, one example and one criticism.

Practise the skills. Plan a short activity and time it. Write an observation record and check it against the facts. Design a corner of a classroom on paper. Practise talking to a parent calmly.

Keep a reflective journal from the first week. Note what happened, what you did and what you would change. This builds the habit that teaching practice and action research require.

Use your country’s official documents. Laws, policies, curricula and quality standards differ by country and change, so check the current official source and give the date.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
sections.text:
Students often treat a theory as a rule. Each theory describes some children in some settings, and each has limits. Another fault is describing children only in terms of deficits instead of strengths.

Many forget that play is learning, not a break from it, and plan activities that are too teacher directed. Some copy activities from other countries without asking whether materials, climate, language or class size fit.

In written work, common faults are unsupported claims about child development, confusing observation with opinion, and ignoring consent and confidentiality when writing about children. Never use a child’s real name in an assignment without permission. In research, a small sample cannot support a broad conclusion.

keyPoints: Early childhood education covers care and learning from birth to about eight years, though the age range differs by country.
Courses combine child development, play, curriculum, health, inclusion, protection, policy and research.
Degree titles, lengths and regulating bodies differ by country, so check your own institution’s handbook.
Play is a main way young children learn, not a break from learning.
Link each theory to a real example and learn its limits as well as its claim.
Protect children’s privacy: do not name a child in written work without permission.

en.title: What Is Early Childhood Education?
en.short: Defines early childhood education, its age range, settings, historical roots and the difference from childcare.

sections.heading: Defining the field
sections.text:
Early childhood education (ECE) is the organised care and teaching of young children before and sometimes during the first years of primary school. Official age ranges vary by country: some systems cover birth to 8 years, others birth to 5 or 6, and some include early primary. Check the current national curriculum or ministry definition.

The field studies how young children learn and how adults can support their development through planned experiences, relationships and routines.

sections.heading: Settings and roots
sections.text:
Provision ranges from home-based care, where a childminder or relative cares for a small group, to crèches, playgroups, nursery schools, preschools, kindergartens and early primary classes. Settings differ in size, funding, staff qualifications and curriculum. In an invented case in Ibadan, Nigeria, a mother uses a nearby home-based childminder for her two-year-old and later a private preschool, while a public primary class follows a state curriculum.

Friedrich Froebel established the kindergarten and emphasised play, songs and structured materials he called gifts. Maria Montessori developed prepared environments (rooms arranged so children can explore independently), self-correcting materials and respect for the child’s independence. John Dewey argued that education should connect to children’s experience and active inquiry. These traditions shaped modern ECE, though practice varies.

sections.heading: Education or childcare
sections.text:
Education is intentional: adults plan experiences that support learning and development. Childcare is the supervision and care that lets parents work or study. The two overlap, because good care includes conversation, play and routines that teach.

A service may be mainly childcare, mainly education, or both; some countries use the term educare for combined provision. Ask what a setting actually does, not only what it is called.

keyPoints: Early childhood education is organised teaching and care for young children, often from birth to about eight years, but official ranges vary by country.
Provision includes home-based care, crèches, playgroups, nurseries, preschools, kindergartens and early primary classes.
Froebel, Montessori and Dewey are key historical influences on the field.
Education is intentional learning support; childcare is supervision and care, and the two often overlap.
Check the current national definition and local rules rather than assuming one age range.

en.title: Child Growth and Development: Conception to Age Eight
en.short: Physical, cognitive, language, social and emotional development from conception to age eight.

sections.heading: Domains and milestones
sections.text:
Development is change in physical, cognitive, language, social and emotional domains. Prenatal development is fast: the brain and body form before birth, and nutrition, infection and toxins can affect it. Physical development includes brain growth, gross motor skills such as sitting and walking, and fine motor skills such as grasping and drawing. Cognitive development includes attention, memory and problem solving; Piaget described sensorimotor learning through senses and actions from birth to about age two and preoperational thinking symbolic but not yet logical from about two to seven. Language moves from cooing and babbling to first words, phrases and sentences. Social and emotional development includes attachment close emotional bond, self-regulation and play with others.

Milestones are typical skills, not deadlines: sitting often around six to eight months, walking around twelve months (a usual range is about nine to eighteen), first words around twelve months, and two-word phrases around eighteen to twenty-four months. Children vary.

sections.heading: Nature, nurture and variation
sections.text:
Nature means genetic inheritance; nurture means everything from nutrition and health care to stimulation, language and culture. They interact: genes shape how a child responds, while care and opportunity shape whether abilities develop. Individual variation is normal and comes from temperament usual style of responding, health, family, language and culture.

Consider Amina, aged three, in a Nigerian town. She says few words but understands instructions and uses gestures. Her teacher records this, checks her hearing and home language, and adds conversation and play. She does not call Amina slow.

sections.heading: Risk, protection and labels
sections.text:
Risk factors increase the chance of poor outcomes: poverty, malnutrition, neglect, violence and unstable care. Protective factors buffer stress: responsive caregiving, good nutrition, safety, play, early learning and community support. Use developmental knowledge to notice and support, not to label.

Labels such as slow or naughty can stick and lower expectations. Instead describe what a child does, when, and in what context; compare with milestones as ranges; and refer for specialist assessment when concerned, working with the family.

keyPoints: Development from conception to about age eight covers physical, cognitive, language, social and emotional domains.
Milestones are typical ranges, not fixed deadlines, and children vary.
Nature (genetics) and nurture (care, nutrition, stimulation and culture) interact.
Risk factors such as poverty and neglect raise the chance of poor outcomes; protective factors such as responsive care buffer them.
Describe behaviour and context rather than using labels such as slow or naughty.
When concerned, compare with milestones, check hearing and language, and refer for specialist assessment with family involvement.

en.title: Learning Theories for Young Children
en.short: A summary of Piaget, Vygotsky, Erikson, Bronfenbrenner, behaviourism and social learning theory in early years.

sections.heading: Constructivist theories
sections.text:
Piaget described children as active learners who build schemas, which are mental patterns for understanding experience. New experience is assimilated into an existing schema or accommodated by changing it. His stages, sensorimotor to formal operational, suggest that tasks must match the child’s thinking. In practice, provide concrete materials and time to explore. Limits: stages are broad, and children often succeed earlier than he claimed.

Vygotsky stressed social learning. The zone of proximal development (ZPD) is the gap between what a child can do alone and what they can do with skilled help. Scaffolding means temporary support, reduced as the child gains control. In practice, model, prompt and work alongside children. Limits: ZPD is hard to measure, and support can become too directive.

sections.heading: Psychosocial and ecological
sections.text:
Erikson’s psychosocial stages pair a task with a social relationship. In early years, trust versus mistrust in infancy and autonomy versus shame and doubt in toddlerhood matter; initiative versus guilt follows in the preschool years. Practice: consistent care, safe choices and praise for effort. Limits: ages are approximate and culture shapes how stages appear.

Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems model places the child inside microsystems such as family and setting, the mesosystem of links between them, the exosystem such as a parent’s workplace, the macrosystem of culture and policy, and the chronosystem of time. Practice: work with families and note wider pressures. Limits: it describes influences more than it predicts development.

sections.heading: Behaviourism and social learning
sections.text:
Behaviourism explains learning through stimulus, response and reinforcement. Positive reinforcement adds something pleasant after a behaviour, making it more likely. Social learning theory, associated with Bandura, adds observation and modelling: children imitate adults and peers, and vicarious reinforcement means seeing others rewarded. Practice: notice and praise wanted behaviour, and model what you expect. Limits: rewards can undermine intrinsic motivation, and children are not passive.

Case: a child refuses to tidy. A practitioner models tidying a box, invites the child to copy, and praises the action. This uses modelling and reinforcement.

keyPoints: Piaget saw children as active learners who build and revise schemas.
Vygotsky’s zone of proximal development is the gap between independent and supported performance.
Erikson linked early tasks to trust, autonomy and initiative.
Bronfenbrenner’s ecological systems range from family to culture and time.
Behaviourism uses reinforcement; social learning theory adds observation and modelling.
Theories guide practice but have limits, so use them critically and observe the child.

en.title: Play and Play-Based Learning
en.short: Types and stages of play, the adult’s role, play for learning, observation and safety.

sections.heading: Types of play
sections.text:
Free play is child-led: the child chooses what, how and with whom. Guided play keeps the child’s interest but an adult adds materials, questions or a gentle challenge. Structured play is adult-directed, with rules or a set goal, such as a throwing game.

Common forms overlap. Pretend play uses symbols: a box becomes a bus. Constructive play builds or makes, as with blocks or clay. Physical play uses large or small movement, such as running or threading. Social play involves others, from sharing materials to cooperative games.

sections.heading: Stages and adult role
sections.text:
Parten’s widely used account describes social stages: unoccupied (not playing), solitary (alone), onlooker (watching), parallel (side by side), associative (sharing without organising) and cooperative (planning roles and rules). Children move between stages; solitary play is not a problem.

The adult observes first, then provides time, space and open materials (items with no fixed use). Scaffolding means giving just enough help, then stepping back. Adults join when invited, model language, and protect play from being taken over. In a Nairobi nursery, teacher Achieng sees two children 'selling' stones. She adds paper notes and a basket, then lets them lead.

sections.heading: Play and learning
sections.text: Play supports learning because the child is active and motivated. Pretend play builds language and story, constructive play builds ideas about space and early maths, physical play builds movement control, and social play builds turn-taking and negotiation. Guided play can target a skill while keeping choice. Play supports self-control as children agree rules and settle disputes.

sections.heading: Watching and keeping safe
sections.text: To observe play, watch quietly, note what the child does and says, and record briefly. Use the notes to plan materials or support, not to label the child. Safety means checking age suitability, choking risks, broken equipment and hygiene, and supervising without hovering. Risk-benefit thinking weighs a manageable challenge against likely harm. Agree boundaries, teach use of tools, and keep first-aid arrangements current.

keyPoints: Free play is child-led, guided play is adult-scaffolded and structured play is adult-directed.
Pretend, constructive, physical and social play often overlap.
Parten’s stages run from solitary to cooperative, and children move between them.
The adult observes, provides materials and scaffolds without taking over.
Play supports language, thinking, movement and social learning.
Keep play safe through supervision, suitable materials and risk-benefit thinking.

en.title: Observation, Assessment and Record Keeping
en.short: Observation methods, ethical recording, and using records to plan for young children.

sections.heading: Why observe
sections.text: Observation means watching and listening carefully to children in everyday activity, then writing down what happened without judging it. It is the base of assessment in early childhood. Formal assessment uses set tasks, tests or standardised scales to compare a child with a standard or with other children. Observation describes learning in context; formal assessment measures it. Both can inform teaching, but observation is better for day-to-day planning because it shows how a child approaches play, language and relationships.

sections.heading: Six methods
sections.text:
Running records are detailed, continuous narratives written during or soon after an episode, with times and direct speech. Anecdotal records are short notes on one specific incident. Event sampling records every time a defined behaviour occurs, such as a child leaving group time. Time sampling records whether a behaviour is present at fixed intervals, for example every five minutes. Checklists list skills or behaviours to tick when seen. Portfolios collect work, photos and notes over time to show progress.

Case: Teacher Amina in Kano wants to understand four-year-old Musa’s block play. She writes a ten-minute running record, adds an anecdotal note when he shares blocks, and keeps photos in his portfolio. She uses a checklist for fine motor skills, not a test.

sections.heading: Ethics and assessment
sections.text: Ethical recording needs family consent where required, confidentiality, secure storage and objective language. Write what a child did, not labels such as lazy. Record only what is needed, share records only with those who need them, and let families see their child’s record. Observation is not formal assessment: it does not rank children or decide school readiness by itself.

sections.heading: From records to planning
sections.text: Records guide planning when teachers review them regularly. They show interests, strengths, gaps and repeated behaviour. Amina sees Musa avoids group tidy-up, so she adds a picture tidy-up chart and a small-group routine. She records again to check whether the change helped. This cycle, observe, record, reflect, plan, act, then observe again, keeps planning responsive rather than fixed.

keyPoints: Observation records what a child does in context; formal assessment uses set tasks or standardised scales.
Running records are detailed narratives; anecdotal records are brief notes on one incident.
Event sampling records every occurrence of a defined behaviour; time sampling checks at fixed intervals.
Checklists tick listed skills; portfolios collect evidence of progress over time.
Ethical recording requires consent where required, confidentiality, secure storage and objective language.
Records guide planning when teachers review them, identify needs and interests, plan, act and observe again.

en.title: Health, Nutrition and Safety in the Early Years
en.short: Health needs, balanced diet, hygiene, sleep, illness referral, safe environments, risk assessment and first aid.

sections.heading: Health and nutrition
sections.text: Young children need enough energy and nutrients to grow, play and fight infection. A balanced diet gives variety from the main food groups: cereals and tubers, pulses (beans, peas and lentils), vegetables and fruit, foods from animals or alternatives, and fats and oils. Offer water often. Cut food small to reduce choking, and check allergies. Health needs include growth monitoring, immunisation and developmental checks. Schedules differ by country, so follow the current national schedule and local setting policy.

sections.heading: Hygiene, sleep, illness
sections.text: Handwashing with soap is the simplest defence against diarrhoea and respiratory infection. Wash hands before food, after toileting and after wiping noses. Clean food surfaces, toys and toilets, and store food safely. Sleep and rest support mood, memory and growth; needs vary with age, so keep a calm routine. Common illnesses include fever, cough, colds, vomiting and diarrhoea. Refer when a child is drowsy, has difficulty breathing, convulsions, severe dehydration, a stiff neck or a rash that does not fade under pressure. Follow local health rules and tell parents.

sections.heading: Safe environments
sections.text: A safe setting lowers the chance of injury without removing reasonable challenge. Indoors, check furniture, stairs, windows, sockets, cleaning products and small objects. Outdoors, check surfaces, gates, water, plants, play equipment and shade. Risk assessment means looking for hazards, judging how likely and how serious harm is, and removing or controlling the risk. Record checks and review them. Supervise closely, especially near water and roads.

sections.heading: First aid and emergencies
sections.text: First aid is immediate, basic care before professional help. Every setting needs trained staff, a stocked kit, clear emergency numbers and written procedures. In an emergency, make the area safe, check response and breathing, call emergency services, and start care within your training. For example, if a child drinks a cleaning product, do not make them vomit; call the poison service or emergency number and follow advice. Report and record every incident.

keyPoints: A balanced diet offers variety from the main food groups, with water and safe food preparation.
Handwashing with soap and clean surfaces reduce the spread of common infections.
Refer a child who is drowsy, struggling to breathe, convulsing, severely dehydrated or has a non-fading rash.
Risk assessment means identifying hazards, judging likelihood and seriousness, then controlling them.
First aid is basic care before professional help; settings need trained staff, a kit and clear emergency procedures.
Immunisation and health check schedules vary by country, so check the current national schedule and local policy.

en.title: Families, Communities and Culture
en.short: Family systems, parenting styles, home-school communication, community resources and cultural diversity.

sections.heading: Family and parenting styles
sections.text:
A family system is the network of relationships in which a child grows up. It may be nuclear, extended, single-parent, blended, foster or child-headed; each shape has strengths, so ask who cares for the child rather than assume.

Parenting styles describe how adults combine warmth with control. Diana Baumrind described authoritative (warm but firm, with reasons), authoritarian (firm, obedience-focused, less warmth) and permissive (warm, few limits) styles. Authoritative parenting is linked with better outcomes in research, but most of that research was Western, and what counts as warmth or control varies by culture.

sections.heading: Home-school communication
sections.text:
Communication with caregivers should be regular, two-way and respectful. Use several routes: a word at drop-off, a notebook, a phone call, a short message, planned meetings, and home visits where policy allows. Keep messages specific, avoid jargon, share successes as well as concerns, and keep confidences.

Barriers include long working hours, travel and cost, language and literacy, past bad experiences of school, and a feeling of not being welcome. Ask families what suits them.

sections.heading: Community resources
sections.text: Every setting sits inside a community with resources: health clinics, libraries, community centres, religious bodies, markets, artisans, elders, playgroups and non-governmental organisations. A resource map, listing each contact and what they offer, helps with visits, referrals and support. Invite community members in as experts, such as a carpenter showing tools or a nurse explaining handwashing.

sections.heading: Culture and religion
sections.text:
Culture shapes feeding, sleep, naming, discipline, play and what adults expect of children. Religion shapes diet, dress, festivals and values. Treat these differences as knowledge, not deficits. Ask caregivers about routines and preferences instead of guessing from a name or language, and check food and festival practices before planning.

Case: Mrs Adeyemi, a nursery teacher, noticed that Chidi’s father, Mr Okoro, missed every meeting. She asked rather than judged: he worked night shifts. She sent a short voice message and a photo of Chidi’s drawing; he replied and came to a Saturday slot.

keyPoints: Families take many forms, and the practitioner should ask who cares for the child.
Parenting styles combine warmth and control; authoritative means warm but firm with reasons.
Research on parenting styles is largely Western, so interpret it with cultural care.
Home-school communication should be regular, two-way, jargon-free and confidential.
Barriers such as work hours, language and past school experience are real; offer choices.
Community resources and cultural knowledge can be built into planning and referrals.

en.title: Language Development and Emergent Literacy
en.short: Oral language, listening, vocabulary, storytelling, sounds, print, early writing and multilingual support.

sections.heading: Oral language and listening
sections.text: Oral language is speaking and understanding speech. Listening is active attention to sounds, words and meaning. Children learn both through conversation, songs, rhymes and questions. Vocabulary is the stock of words a child knows and uses; it grows when adults name things, explain words and read aloud. A child who hears many words in real situations learns meanings, not just labels.

sections.heading: Stories and sounds
sections.text: Storytelling means telling or reading a story with expression, pauses and questions. It builds comprehension, memory and a love of language. Phonological awareness is awareness of the sounds of speech apart from meaning: hearing syllables, rhymes and first sounds. It is not the same as phonics, which links letters to sounds. A simple game: clap the syllables in “A-mi-na” (three claps), then ask which name rhymes with “Bello”.

sections.heading: Print and early writing
sections.text: Print concepts are the rules of written language: print carries meaning, words are read left to right in English, and pages have front and back. Emergent writing is children’s early marks, scribbles, invented spellings and letter-like forms before conventional writing. Adults support it by providing paper, crayons, signs and labels, and by writing children’s spoken words down. Do not correct every mark; praise the attempt and model the adult form.

sections.heading: Multilingual learning and adults
sections.text: Multilingual development means growing in two or more languages. Children can learn a home language and a school language together; strong home language supports the second. Adults help by speaking clearly, waiting, listening, using gestures and repeating key words in context. Formal drilling, such as repeating lists or copying letters without meaning, differs from rich language learning, which uses play, stories, conversation and purpose. In a Kano nursery, Mr Bello reads a picture book, pauses for children to predict, and lets them tell the story in Hausa before trying English words.

keyPoints: Oral language and listening grow through conversation, songs, rhymes and read-alouds.
Vocabulary is the stock of words a child understands and uses.
Phonological awareness is awareness of speech sounds; phonics links letters to sounds.
Print concepts are rules of written language, and emergent writing includes scribbles and invented spellings.
Multilingual children benefit when home language is valued and adults model and repeat words in context.
Rich language learning uses play, stories and purpose, while formal drilling without meaning is less effective.

en.title: Early Mathematics and Science Foundations
en.short: Number sense, counting, shapes, patterns, measurement, sorting, and inquiry through everyday play.

sections.heading: Number sense and counting
sections.text:
Number sense is a feel for how numbers work: a number names a quantity, quantities can be compared, and numbers can be combined and separated. Counting has two parts. Rote counting is saying number names in order. Meaningful counting links each number word to one object, called one-to-one correspondence. The last number said tells how many, called cardinality. Use real objects.

Example: Ada lines up five bottle caps. She touches each cap once and says one, two, three, four, five. Asked how many, she says five. Giving one cap to each of five friends shows one-to-one correspondence without counting.

sections.heading: Shapes, patterns and measurement
sections.text:
Shapes are named by features. A circle is round with no corners; a triangle has three straight sides; a square has four equal sides and four right angles. Children learn shapes by handling blocks, tins and cloth, and finding them in rooms and outdoors. A pattern is a repeated arrangement, such as red, blue, red, blue. Copying and continuing patterns builds early algebraic thinking.

Measurement compares an attribute, such as length, weight, capacity or time, using direct comparison or non-standard units. A child may find a table is six hand-spans long. Sorting groups objects by one attribute; comparison states how they differ, for example longer, heavier or more. Use spoons, stones, cups and water.

sections.heading: Inquiry through play
sections.text:
Inquiry begins with noticing and asking questions. Observation means using the senses carefully to gather evidence. Prediction is a guess based on what a child knows; testing checks it. Cause and effect is the link between an action and what follows. Adults ask open questions: What will happen if we add water? Why do you think so?

Case: Ben and Chidi compare a dry sponge and a wet sponge. They predict the wet one will be heavier. They lift both. The wet one feels heavier, so they observe that water adds weight. This is early science through play, not a formal experiment. Record the children’s words.

keyPoints: Number sense links number names to quantities and helps children compare and combine numbers.
One-to-one correspondence means matching one object or number word to exactly one item.
Cardinality means the last number counted tells the size of the set.
Shapes are defined by features, and patterns are repeated arrangements that children can copy and continue.
Measurement compares attributes using direct comparison or non-standard units, while sorting groups by one attribute.
Inquiry uses observation, prediction and testing to explore cause and effect through everyday play.

en.title: Curriculum Planning and Environment Design
en.short: Curriculum models, long, medium and short term planning, routines, indoor and outdoor spaces, materials and safety.

sections.heading: Models and frameworks
sections.text: A curriculum model is an organised set of beliefs and practices about what children learn and how adults support it. Montessori, from Maria Montessori in Italy, stresses a prepared environment, mixed ages, child-led activity and self-correcting materials. Reggio Emilia, from northern Italy, sees the child as capable, uses long projects, documentation and the environment as a third teacher. HighScope, from the United States, uses active learning, a plan-do-review cycle and a consistent daily routine. Treat these as examples to adapt, not recipes.

sections.heading: Three planning levels
sections.text: Planning works at three levels. A long-term plan is an annual or termly overview of goals, themes and resources. A medium-term plan breaks those goals into weeks or half-terms. A short-term plan is the daily or weekly detail: activities, grouping, materials, adult role and observation. For example, Mrs Adeyemi in Ibadan plans a term on markets. Her long-term goal is sorting and counting produce. Medium-term weeks cover fruit, grains and transport. One short-term day uses a market stall, bean sorting and an outdoor delivery route.

sections.heading: Routines and spaces
sections.text: Routines give security. A predictable sequence for arrival, group time, free play, snack, rest, outdoor play, tidy-up and home helps children know what comes next. Warn before transitions and keep waiting short. Indoor space needs quiet, active, messy and role-play zones. Outdoor space needs shade, safe surfaces, open ground and storage. Materials should be open-ended, age-appropriate, accessible and rotated. Safety means supervision, risk assessment, secure fencing, hazard checks, first aid and allergy control.

sections.heading: Alignment and review
sections.text: Alignment means mapping planned activities to the national or state early years framework, not just adding themes. Check the current official document, because learning areas, ratios and space rules differ by country and change. Record how each activity meets a stated goal, and keep evidence for inspection. Review plans with colleagues and families, and adjust for children’s interests and needs.

keyPoints: Curriculum models such as Montessori, Reggio Emilia and HighScope are frameworks to adapt, not fixed recipes.
Long-term plans give annual or termly goals; medium-term plans break them into weeks; short-term plans detail daily activities and materials.
Predictable routines and warned transitions help young children feel secure.
Indoor and outdoor spaces should have defined zones, accessible open-ended materials and safe surfaces.
Safety planning includes supervision, risk assessment, secure fencing, hazard checks, first aid and allergy control.
Map every planned activity to the current national or state early years framework and keep evidence.

en.title: Language, Literacy and Multilingual Pedagogy
en.short: Advanced methods for oral language, vocabulary, comprehension, phonics, reading aloud, writing and multilingual support.

sections.heading: Balanced literacy teaching
sections.text: Balanced literacy combines code-focused and meaning-focused teaching. Phonological awareness is the ability to hear and work with sounds in spoken words, such as syllables and rhymes. Phonics teaches how letters map to sounds. Advanced oral language work uses rich conversation, explicit vocabulary instruction with child-friendly definitions, and repeated exposure in different contexts. Comprehension improves when teachers model strategies: predicting, questioning, clarifying and summarising. Reading aloud becomes dialogic when the teacher pauses to ask open questions and lets children talk. Writing follows a process of planning, drafting, revising and editing, with modelled and shared writing before independent work.

sections.heading: Multilingual classrooms
sections.text: Multilingual classrooms treat the home language as a resource, not a problem. Translanguaging means letting children use all their languages to understand and express ideas. A teacher may read a story in the home language, discuss it, then bridge key words into the school language. Policy differs by country: some systems encourage early home-language literacy, others move quickly to an official language. Check local curriculum guidance. The aim is additive bilingualism, where the second language is added without replacing the first.

sections.heading: Assessment and support
sections.text: Assessment should be formative and frequent. Running records capture a child’s oral reading, and miscue analysis examines whether errors keep meaning. Short phonological awareness and vocabulary checks identify gaps. Support struggling children with explicit small-group teaching, more practice, modelled reading and scaffolded writing. Response to intervention (RTI) is one tiered framework used in some countries; local policy varies. A case: Mrs Adeyemi in Ibadan notices Tunde, a Yoruba-speaking child, reads slowly in English. She pairs him with a fluent partner for repeated reading, pre-teaches five key words in Yoruba and English, and checks his progress weekly. After four weeks he reads with fewer meaning-changing errors.

keyPoints: Balanced literacy combines code-focused work (phonological awareness, phonics) with meaning-focused work (oral language, vocabulary, comprehension, writing).
Explicit vocabulary teaching gives child-friendly definitions and repeated encounters in different contexts.
Dialogic reading aloud pauses for open questions and child talk.
Multilingual pedagogy uses the home language as a resource and may use translanguaging; policy varies by country.
Formative assessment such as running records and miscue analysis guides support.
Struggling readers need explicit small-group teaching, more practice and scaffolded tasks, with progress checked.

en.title: Early Mathematics Pedagogy
en.short: Covers number, operations, geometry, measurement, patterns, data, talk, games, misconceptions, assessment, inclusion.

sections.heading: Number and operations
sections.text: Number work begins with counting principles: stable order, one-to-one correspondence and cardinality, the idea that the last number tells how many. Subitising, instantly recognising small quantities, supports fluency. Children build part-part-whole knowledge with manipulatives, concrete objects such as counters or blocks, then pictures and symbols. Worked example: share 12 counters equally among 3 trays. Each tray gets 12 ÷ 3 = 4 counters. Check: 3 × 4 = 12. Ask the child to explain the sharing.

sections.heading: Geometry, measurement, patterns
sections.text: Geometry covers shape properties and spatial reasoning: composing and decomposing shapes, position words and puzzles. Measurement starts with direct comparison, such as longer or heavier, then non-standard units, such as hand spans or cubes, before standard units. Patterns include repeating patterns, such as red, blue, red, blue, and growing patterns such as 2, 4, 6, 8, so the next term is 10. Early data work uses sorting, tally marks and picture charts to answer a simple question.

sections.heading: Talk, games, misconceptions
sections.text: Mathematical talk means using precise words for quantity, shape, position and comparison. Open questions, think-alouds and paired explanation make reasoning visible. Games add repeated practice with rules and feedback. Problem solving should use familiar stories and real objects, so children decide what to do. Common misconceptions include losing one-to-one correspondence when counting, thinking a taller container always holds more, and treating a square turned on its corner as a different shape. Notice the error, ask for explanation, and offer a contrasting example.

sections.heading: Assessment and inclusion
sections.text: Assessment should be observational and ongoing: watch counting, questioning, work samples and practical tasks. Record what a child can do independently and what needs support. Avoid timed tests that reward speed. Inclusive participation means multiple ways to respond, accessible manipulatives, large print or tactile shapes, flexible grouping, and contexts from home and community. Plan support for children with disabilities and for those who are anxious, and keep expectations high with scaffolds.

keyPoints: Counting depends on stable order, one-to-one correspondence and cardinality.
Manipulatives and pictures bridge concrete experience and written symbols.
For equal sharing, total ÷ number of groups = each share; check by groups × each = total.
Geometry, measurement, patterns and early data are taught through comparison, sorting and practical tasks.
Mathematical talk and games make reasoning visible and give repeated practice.
Notice misconceptions, assess by observation, and plan inclusive ways to participate.

en.title: Early Science and Inquiry Pedagogy
en.short: The inquiry cycle, questioning, experiments, nature study, STEM, documentation, talk, safety and inclusion.

sections.heading: Inquiry cycle
sections.text: Inquiry is learning by investigating questions, not memorising answers. A common cycle has five phases: engage, explore, explain, elaborate and evaluate, often called the 5E model. Engage presents a puzzle. Explore lets children handle materials. Explain puts observations into words. Elaborate applies the idea in a new situation. Evaluate reviews what changed in thinking. The cycle is not rigid; children may return to exploring.

sections.heading: Questions and talk
sections.text: Questioning drives inquiry. Open questions, such as 'What do you notice?' or 'What might happen if...?', invite many answers. Closed questions check facts. Productive questions focus on action, comparison or prediction. Give wait time, and let children answer in words, drawing or gesture. Scientific talk means modelling words like observe, predict, compare, measure and explain. The adult can restate a child’s idea: 'You think the ice will melt faster in the sun.' This supports reasoning without giving the answer.

sections.heading: Experiments and nature
sections.text: Hands-on experiments should be simple, safe and repeatable. Children can test whether seeds need light, which paper towel absorbs most water, or how ramp angle changes speed. A fair test changes one thing and keeps others the same. Nature study means regular observation of plants, weather, insects and soil locally. Children record changes and learn to respect living things. In a case, Teacher Amina in Kano gives pairs a dry bean and a wet bean. Children predict, observe for three days, draw, and say what changed.

sections.heading: STEM, safety, inclusion
sections.text: STEM integration links science with technology, engineering and mathematics through real problems: build a bridge for a toy car, measure the span, improve the design. Documentation makes learning visible. Use photographs, children’s drawings, dictated captions and a simple display. Safety comes first: assess risks, supervise tools, check allergies, teach handwashing and never taste unknown materials. Inclusion means every child can join. Offer adapted tools, visual supports, roles for children with disabilities, and home-language words. Avoid assuming who is 'good at science'.

keyPoints: Inquiry follows a cycle such as engage, explore, explain, elaborate and evaluate, not a fixed recipe.
Open and productive questions, with wait time, invite children to predict, compare and explain.
Hands-on tests and nature study should be safe, repeatable and respectful of living things.
Scientific talk is modelled by adults using words such as observe, predict, compare and explain.
STEM integration connects science to real design and measurement problems.
Documentation and inclusive planning make inquiry visible and open to every child.

en.title: Social and Emotional Learning and Guidance
en.short: Attachment, self-regulation, empathy, conflict, guidance, positive behaviour support and trauma-sensitive practice.

sections.heading: Attachment and self-regulation
sections.text:
Attachment is the lasting emotional bond between a child and caregiver. A secure attachment gives the child a safe base for exploring and returning for comfort. Adults build it by responding warmly and predictably: child signals, adult answers.

Self-regulation is the ability to manage feelings, attention and behaviour to suit the situation. Young children borrow adult calm before they can do this alone; this is co-regulation. Teach it through naming feelings, breathing and clear routines, not by demanding that a child 'calm down' unaided.

sections.heading: Empathy, friendships and conflict
sections.text:
Empathy is understanding and sharing another person’s feelings. It grows through perspective taking, stories and adults naming feelings without shaming. Friendships need turn taking, joining in and repairing mistakes.

Conflict is normal. Teach a short routine: stop, say the problem, say how you feel, suggest a solution, agree. For example, in Mrs Adeyemi’s nursery class in Ibadan, two children pull at one truck. She helps them say, 'I feel angry because I want a turn,' then agree a two-minute timer. Guidance teaches the skill; punishment only suppresses.

sections.heading: Guidance and positive behaviour
sections.text:
Guidance means teaching expected behaviour rather than punishing mistakes. Positive behaviour support (PBS) is a framework that sets a few clear expectations, teaches routines, praises what you want and changes the environment before blaming the child. Classroom climate is the emotional tone: safe, predictable, respectful and inclusive.

Punishment such as shaming or exclusion may stop a behaviour briefly but does not teach a replacement. Use natural or logical consequences, restore relationships and keep the child’s dignity.

sections.heading: Trauma-sensitive practice and families
sections.text:
Trauma-sensitive practice assumes some children have lived through frightening events. It offers predictable routines, warning before changes, quiet choices, calm adult voices and no public shaming. It is not therapy and does not require a diagnosis.

Work with families as partners: ask about home routines, share observations, agree consistent responses and respect the family’s language and culture. Policies and referral routes differ by country, so check local guidance and your setting’s safeguarding lead.

keyPoints: Attachment is a lasting bond; a secure base supports exploration and comfort seeking.
Self-regulation develops through co-regulation, naming feelings and predictable routines.
Empathy and friendship skills are taught through perspective taking and turn taking.
Conflict can be handled with a short problem-solving routine rather than blame.
Positive behaviour support teaches expectations and changes the environment instead of punishing.
Trauma-sensitive practice and family partnership make guidance consistent and calm.

en.title: Creative Arts, Music and Movement
en.short: Children’s art stages, process and product, music, rhythm, dance, drama, materials and fair assessment.

sections.heading: Art stages and process
sections.text: Widely used accounts, such as Lowenfeld’s, describe children moving from scribbling and exploration to first representational forms, then to more organised symbols. Ages vary, so observe the child rather than the calendar. Process art values exploration, choice and problem solving. Product art aims at a set result, such as a copied craft. Both can appear, but templates and adult-made models tend to reduce children’s decisions. Offer open-ended materials: paper, paint, clay, fabric, safe recycled boxes, natural items. Ask about the work and record the child’s ideas.

sections.heading: Music rhythm and movement
sections.text: Music activities include singing, chanting, clapping and simple instruments. Beat is the steady pulse; rhythm is the pattern of long and short sounds and silences; tempo is speed. Children can keep a beat with body percussion, drums or homemade shakers. Dance develops body awareness, space, time and effort. Let children move freely and invent sequences, not only copy steps. Use local songs, languages and instruments where possible, and ask families for favourites. Adapt instruments and movements for disabled children.

sections.heading: Drama and imaginative play
sections.text: Drama and imaginative play let children try roles, stories and feelings. Provide puppets, scarves, boxes and a simple corner for a shop, clinic or home. Teacher-in-role, where the adult joins a fictional role briefly, can extend play without taking it over. In an invented case, Amina, a nursery teacher in Kano, Nigeria, sets up a market with recycled boxes and local cloth. She watches children negotiate roles and make signs, then notes what they solve together.

sections.heading: Assessment and inclusion
sections.text: Assessment should gather evidence without ranking products. Use photos, short notes and children’s comments. Look for engagement, persistence, use of materials, cooperation and expressive choices. Do not grade neatness or reward one child’s picture as best. Inclusive and culturally responsive practice means safe, non-toxic materials, accessible tools, and images and songs that reflect children’s lives without stereotypes. Check local health and safety rules. The aim is confidence and expression, not a perfect product.

keyPoints: Children’s art usually moves from exploration and scribbling towards more organised representation, but ages vary.
Process art values choice and problem solving; product art aims at a set result, and templates can limit learning.
Beat is the steady pulse, rhythm is the pattern of sounds and silences, and tempo is speed.
Dance and drama support expression, body awareness, role taking and cooperation.
Use open-ended, safe and culturally familiar materials, and adapt activities for disabled children.
Assess through observation, photos and children’s comments, not by ranking neatness or conformity.

en.title: Physical Development and Outdoor Learning
en.short: Gross and fine motor skills, perceptual-motor development, outdoor play, risk-benefit assessment and inclusion.

sections.heading: Gross and fine motor skills
sections.text:
Gross motor skills use the large muscles: walking, running, climbing, jumping, throwing. Fine motor skills use the small muscles of the hands: grasping, the pincer grip (thumb and forefinger), threading, drawing, fastening buttons. Control generally develops from the head downwards and from the centre outwards, so arm control comes before finger control.

Perceptual-motor skills link the senses to movement: hand-eye coordination, balance, body awareness and spatial awareness. They underpin handwriting and ball games. Fundamental movement skills are grouped as locomotor (running, hopping), stability (balancing) and manipulative (catching, kicking).

sections.heading: Active play outdoors
sections.text:
Children learn to move by moving, so practice matters more than instruction. The World Health Organization publishes daily physical activity guidelines for young children; check the current version for your age group. Outdoor play supports activity through space, uneven ground and permission to be vigorous.

Outdoors also brings nature learning: watching ants, planting beans, collecting leaves, noticing weather. Loose parts, meaning open-ended materials such as crates, tyres, planks and cloth, invite building and repeated problem solving. Adults help most by giving time, materials and a few open questions.

sections.heading: Risk and safety
sections.text:
Risk-benefit assessment weighs the developmental benefit of an activity against the chance and seriousness of harm, then cuts the risk without removing the benefit. It is a written, reasoned judgement, not a ban.

Case: staff at a nursery in Kano want planks and crates for balancing. They record the benefits (balance, confidence, cooperation), the hazards (falls onto concrete, trapped fingers) and the controls (move to grass, check wood for splinters, an adult nearby, rules agreed with the children). Daily checks, shade, drinking water and sun protection belong in the routine.

sections.heading: Including every child
sections.text: Children with disabilities should join outdoor play, not watch it. Adapt the equipment (larger, lighter balls, shorter bats), the rules (slower pace, a partner) and the space (firm paths, ramps, shade). A child using a wheelchair can be the caller in a chasing game. Ask the child and family what helps, and check the outdoor area is reachable and usable.

keyPoints: Gross motor skills use large muscles; fine motor skills use the small muscles of the hands.
Perceptual-motor skills link the senses to movement and support handwriting and ball games.
Children need daily physical activity and outdoor time, not only indoor lessons.
Risk-benefit assessment records benefits, hazards and controls, and keeps the activity rather than banning it.
Loose parts and contact with nature support open-ended outdoor learning.
Adapt equipment, rules and space so children with disabilities take part fully.

en.title: Inclusive Practice and Children with Disabilities
en.short: Disability, early referral, adaptations, teamwork, and inclusion versus integration and segregation.

sections.heading: Disability and delay
sections.text: Disability is a long-term physical, sensory, intellectual, learning, communication or behavioural difference that can limit participation. Examples include cerebral palsy, hearing or vision loss, Down syndrome, autism and speech difficulties. Developmental delay means a child is behind expected milestones in one or more areas, such as movement, speech or social interaction. Delay is not the same as disability: some catch up, others need support. Milestone ages vary; use screening tools and professional judgement.

sections.heading: Early identification
sections.text: Early identification means noticing a concern through observation, parent report and screening, then acting promptly. Record what the child can do and what is hard. Share concerns with families plainly and respectfully, and listen to their views. With consent, refer to health, speech therapy, audiology, psychology or other services. Referral is a formal request to a specialist service for assessment or support. Do not wait for a diagnosis before making simple adaptations. Keep records confidential; follow local rules.

sections.heading: Adapting the setting
sections.text: Adaptation changes the setting so the child can take part. Physical changes include ramps, clear pathways, lighting and quiet spaces. Materials may need larger print, tactile objects, picture symbols, simple language or assistive technology, meaning devices that help function. Routines work best when predictable: use visual schedules, warn before changes, allow extra time, and break tasks into small steps. In Ibadan, four-year-old Tunde has difficulty hearing. His teacher faces him, uses gestures and pictures, and seats him away from the door. The whole class benefits.

sections.heading: Inclusion and teamwork
sections.text: Segregation places children with disabilities in separate settings. Integration places a child in a mainstream setting but expects the child to fit unchanged arrangements. Inclusion goes further: the setting changes so every child belongs, participates and is supported, with reasonable accommodation (changes that are needed and do not create an undue burden). Teamwork with families and specialists is central: share observations and agree goals. Respect consent and confidentiality. The UN Convention on the Rights of Persons with Disabilities supports inclusion, but national law differs; check local policy.

keyPoints: Disability is a long-term difference that can limit participation; developmental delay is behind expected milestones and may or may not become disability.
Early identification uses observation, family report and screening, then prompt referral with consent.
Adapt environments, materials and routines so the child can take part, not just be present.
Segregation separates children; integration places them in mainstream settings unchanged; inclusion changes the setting so all belong and participate.
Work with families and specialists through shared observations, agreed goals and confidentiality.
Check local law and services, as national policy on inclusive education differs.

en.title: Child Protection and Safeguarding in Early Years
en.short: Types and signs of abuse, safeguarding duties, safe recruitment, disclosure and reporting.

sections.heading: Types and signs
sections.text: Abuse is harm done to a child by an adult or another child. It may be physical, emotional or sexual. Neglect is the ongoing failure to meet a child’s basic needs, such as food, warmth, safety, medical care or affection. Signs include unexplained injuries, fear, withdrawal, poor hygiene, hunger or sexual knowledge beyond the child’s age. Signs are indicators, not proof. Record and report them.

sections.heading: Safeguarding duties
sections.text: Safeguarding means the actions a setting takes to protect children’s health, development and wellbeing and prevent harm. Child protection is the part for children at risk. Duties include a written policy, a named safeguarding lead, a code of conduct, risk assessments, secure records and a clear reporting route. Staff must know the policy and act on concerns, even low-level ones. Legal duties and agencies differ by country, so check current national and local guidance.

sections.heading: Recruitment and supervision
sections.text: Safe recruitment reduces the risk of unsuitable adults working with children. It includes checking identity, qualifications and references, asking about gaps in employment, and using criminal record checks where the law allows. Induction, probation and regular supervision support staff. Supervision means planned, supportive meetings and observation of practice, not surveillance. Settings limit situations where an adult is alone with a child, keep visitor records, and encourage staff to raise concerns about colleagues.

sections.heading: Disclosure and reporting
sections.text: If a child discloses, stay calm and listen. Do not promise secrecy. Explain that you must tell someone who can help. Do not investigate or ask leading questions. Record the child’s exact words, date, time, and sign it. Report promptly to the designated safeguarding lead or local child protection agency. Share information only with those who need it. Confidentiality is not absolute when a child may be at risk. Amina, four, has a burn and says, 'Uncle did it, don’t tell.' The practitioner records and reports it; the lead follows procedure and decides whether parents can be informed.

keyPoints: Abuse may be physical, emotional or sexual; neglect is failure to meet basic needs.
Signs are indicators, not proof; record and report them.
Safeguarding duties include policy, a named lead, a code of conduct, risk assessment and secure records.
Safe recruitment checks identity, qualifications, references and criminal records where the law allows.
When a child discloses, listen, do not promise secrecy, do not investigate, and record exact words.
Report promptly under local procedure and share information only on a need-to-know basis; laws and agencies differ by country.

en.title: Infant and Toddler Care
en.short: Attachment, key-person care, feeding, sleep, hygiene, ratios and early language and motor support.

sections.heading: Attachment and key person
sections.text: Attachment is the enduring emotional bond an infant forms with a few familiar caregivers. Secure attachment grows from consistent, warm responses to cues such as crying, reaching or turning away. A key-person system assigns each child one named practitioner who builds that relationship and coordinates care, while other staff support. Responsive interaction means noticing a cue, interpreting it and answering promptly and appropriately, for example returning a smile, copying a sound or offering comfort before distress escalates.

sections.heading: Daily care routines
sections.text: Feeding should be responsive: watch for hunger cues such as rooting (turning the head towards a touch on the cheek) or hand-to-mouth movements, and fullness cues such as turning away. Hold babies during bottle feeds; never prop a bottle. Follow current health guidance on breastmilk, formula and when to start complementary foods. For sleep, place infants on their back on a firm, flat surface free of soft bedding, and check them regularly. Change nappies promptly, clean front to back, wash hands before and after, and never leave a child unattended on a changing surface. Hygiene includes handwashing, cleaning toys and surfaces, and cleaning feeding equipment as advised.

sections.heading: Groups and ratios
sections.text: Group size is the number of children in a room or class; ratio is the number of children per adult. National rules and accreditation standards set these, and they vary by country and by age, so check the current official source. In general, younger children need smaller groups and more adults per child. Worked example: if a toddler room has 9 children and the local rule is 1 adult to 3 children, the minimum is 9 ÷ 3 = 3 adults. Ratios are a floor, not a target; mixed ages and children with additional needs may require more staff.

sections.heading: Language and movement
sections.text: Talk, sing and narrate daily actions, pause for the child’s sounds, and read simple books face to face. For movement, provide supervised tummy time, floor play and safe space to reach, roll, crawl and pull up. Avoid forcing walking; follow the child’s readiness and check developmental concerns with health professionals.

keyPoints: Secure attachment grows from consistent, warm responses to an infant’s cues.
A key-person system gives each child one named practitioner who coordinates care.
Responsive feeding, safe sleep on the back, prompt nappy changes and handwashing are core routines.
Group size and ratios vary by country and age; check current official standards.
Minimum adults = number of children ÷ children per adult, for example 9 ÷ 3 = 3.
Talk, sing, read and allow supervised floor play to support language and movement.

en.title: Child Assessment and School Readiness
en.short: Purposes and methods of assessment, school readiness, transition, reporting and ethical cautions.

sections.heading: Purposes and methods
sections.text: Assessment is the systematic gathering of information about a child’s learning and development. It is used to plan teaching, identify children who need support, monitor progress, report to families and account for funding. Formative assessment is ongoing and feeds into the next activity. Summative assessment summarises achievement at the end of a period. Screening is a brief check that flags possible delay; it is not a diagnosis and must lead to further assessment. A portfolio is a planned collection of work, photos and comments over time, showing progress rather than one moment. Good assessment uses several methods, including observation and play-based tasks, and is fair across languages and cultures.

sections.heading: School readiness
sections.text: School readiness is more than knowing letters and numbers. It includes physical health, social and emotional confidence, language, self-help skills and a supportive family and school. Readiness is also a property of the school: welcoming settings and age-appropriate expectations matter. Transition into primary school works best when nursery and primary teachers share information with parents’ consent, children visit the new school, and routines are introduced gradually. Entry ages and readiness checks differ by country and school, so check current local policy.

sections.heading: Reporting and labelling
sections.text: Reports to parents should be regular, clear and respectful. Give specific examples of what the child can do, then next steps. Avoid jargon and compare the child with their own earlier progress, not only with others. Keep records confidential and share them only with consent or as the law requires. Avoid harmful labelling: “slow” or “naughty” is a judgement, not a need, and can lower expectations. Describe the behaviour or skill and the support to follow. Do not coach children for tests. Test coaching narrows the curriculum, raises stress and can make results invalid. Example: Mrs Okafor notices that five-year-old Ada hides during group time. She records the behaviour, tries a small-group role, and reviews progress in Ada’s portfolio. She avoids labelling Ada or using practice tests.

keyPoints: Assessment gathers evidence to plan teaching, identify needs, monitor progress and report.
Formative assessment is ongoing; summative assessment summarises a period; screening flags possible needs but is not diagnosis.
Portfolios show progress over time through collected work and comments.
School readiness includes health, social-emotional skills, language, self-help and supportive homes and schools, not only academic skills.
Transition works best with information sharing, visits and gradual routines, with parents’ consent.
Reports should be clear, specific and confidential; avoid labels and test coaching.

en.title: Digital Technology in Early Childhood
en.short: Digital tools, screen-time guidance, app choice, safety, access and a critical view of tech claims.

sections.heading: Tools and their role
sections.text: Digital tools in early childhood are devices and software used with or by young children: tablets, phones, cameras, audio recorders and their apps. They help when they extend real activity, such as photographing a seedling daily to show change. Open-ended tools, which the child controls, are generally preferred to drill apps that only reward correct taps. Technology is one material among many, not a substitute for play, talk or outdoor time.

sections.heading: Screens and health
sections.text: Screen time is time spent looking at a screen. The World Health Organization’s 2019 guidelines for children under 5 recommend no sedentary screen time below age 2, and no more than 1 hour a day at ages 2 to 4, with less being better. In the United States, the American Academy of Pediatrics advises avoiding screens other than video chatting before 18 months. Guidance differs by country. Co-viewing, meaning an adult watching and talking with the child, matters as much as the clock. Screen use close to bedtime is linked to poorer sleep.

sections.heading: Choosing apps
sections.text: Judge an app on the age it suits, whether it is open-ended, adverts and in-app purchases, what data it collects, offline use, language and accessibility. Vendor claims that an app is educational usually lack independent evidence; ask who funded the study. Test it yourself, then watch a child use it. Plan the numbers: 24 children with 4 tablets gives 24 ÷ 4 = 6 children per device; at 10 minutes each, one rotation takes 6 × 10 = 60 minutes.

sections.heading: Safety, equity, claims
sections.text: Digital safety covers children’s data and images, supervision of online contact, and persuasive design, meaning features built to keep a child tapping or to push purchases. Get written parental consent before publishing a photo. Data protection law differs by country; in Nigeria the Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 applies. Equity of access means some homes have devices, fast internet and electricity and some do not; apps in the child’s home language and shared devices in the setting narrow the gap.

keyPoints: Digital tools help most when they extend real activity and the child controls them.
WHO 2019 guidance: no sedentary screen time under age 2, and no more than 1 hour a day at ages 2 to 4, with less being better.
Co-viewing and talking with an adult matter as much as the amount of screen time.
Judge apps on age fit, open-endedness, adverts, data collection, language and accessibility, and test them first.
Vendor claims about learning usually lack independent evidence.
Digital safety includes consent for images and data protection, and unequal access shapes who benefits.

en.title: Early Childhood Policy and Governance
en.short: How early childhood education is organised, regulated, funded and inspected, with country examples.

sections.heading: Who governs
sections.text: Governance means the rules, bodies and processes that steer a service. Early childhood education (ECE) is organised at several levels: national government sets law, policy, curriculum and minimum standards; state, provincial or county governments may register and fund settings; local authorities, private owners and community groups run them. In Kenya, the 2010 Constitution makes pre-primary education a county function, while national bodies set curriculum and quality standards. In England, the Department for Education sets the statutory Early Years Foundation Stage (EYFS), and Ofsted registers and inspects providers. Nigeria has federal, state and local roles, with private, community and faith-based providers active; check current policy.

sections.heading: Curriculum and standards
sections.text: A curriculum framework is an official statement of what children should learn and how adults should teach. England’s EYFS framework is statutory; New Zealand’s Te Whāriki is an early childhood curriculum; Sweden has a national preschool curriculum. Minimum standards are registration rules covering staff qualifications, adult-child ratios, space, health, safety and safeguarding. Ratios vary by age and country; check current rules. Inspection checks compliance and quality: Ofsted in England, the Education Review Office in New Zealand, and the Swedish Schools Inspectorate.

sections.heading: Funding and providers
sections.text: Funding models are supply-side, demand-side or mixed. Supply-side funding gives grants or contracts to providers. Demand-side funding gives parents subsidies, vouchers or funded hours. Sweden funds preschool mainly through municipalities and caps parental fees. England funds early education hours for eligible children and has private and voluntary settings. In Nigeria, government, private, community and faith-based providers coexist, and fees are common. Private providers may be for-profit or non-profit. Communities often run centres and parent committees; regulation should cover all providers.

sections.heading: A registration case
sections.text: Amina wants to open a centre in Kisumu County, Kenya. She applies to the county education office for approval, follows national curriculum guidance, and must meet staffing, space and safety standards. She charges fees, may seek county support, and works with a parent committee. The county inspects the centre and may require improvements.

keyPoints: Governance is multi-level: national bodies set policy and standards, while local, private and community providers deliver services.
A curriculum framework states official learning goals and pedagogy, as in England’s EYFS, New Zealand’s Te Whāriki and Sweden’s preschool curriculum.
Minimum standards are registration rules on qualifications, ratios, space, health, safety and safeguarding, and they vary by country and age group.
Inspection checks compliance and quality, for example by Ofsted in England, the Education Review Office in New Zealand and the Swedish Schools Inspectorate.
Funding can be supply-side grants to providers, demand-side subsidies to parents, or mixed, as in Sweden, England and Nigeria.
Government, private providers and communities all have roles, and regulation should cover every provider.

en.title: Leadership and Management of Early Years Settings
en.short: Running a nursery, preschool or day-care centre: staffing, ratios, budgets, records, supervision, parents and regulators.

sections.heading: Leading and managing
sections.text:
Leadership sets direction, values and culture. Management runs systems that keep the setting safe and solvent: staffing, money, records and compliance. A nursery or day-care centre needs both. The manager is accountable for legal duties even when tasks are delegated.

Agree a simple improvement plan, communicate decisions, and check they are carried out. Good leaders listen to staff and parents, model professional conduct, and keep safeguarding central.

sections.heading: Staffing and supervision
sections.text:
Staffing means enough adults, with the right qualifications, in the right places. Adult-to-child ratios are the minimum number of adults required for a number of children. Regulators set ratios; they vary by country and by children’s ages, so check current official rules. Build the rota with cover for breaks, sickness and training.

Supervision is regular, recorded line management: meetings, observation, appraisal and safeguarding support. Staff development, or continuing professional development (CPD), includes induction, first aid, child protection training, coaching and reflective meetings. Base training on the improvement plan and each person’s goals.

sections.heading: Budgets and records
sections.text:
Budgeting plans income and spending. Income may come from fees, grants or donations. Costs include wages, rent, food, utilities, toys and insurance. A budget should show a surplus for reserves. Example: 40 children × 20,000 = 800,000 income. Wages 440,000 + rent 150,000 + food 100,000 + utilities 60,000 = 750,000 costs, leaving 50,000. Figures are illustrative; use your own currency and current prices.

Records include attendance registers, accident and medication logs, staff files, accounts and children’s records. Keep them accurate, secure and confidential under your country’s data protection law.

sections.heading: Parents and regulators
sections.text:
Work with parents as partners: explain routines, share progress, listen to concerns and use a clear complaints procedure. A settling-in plan helps child and family adjust. Keep confidentiality and record agreed actions.

Regulators register and inspect settings against standards, checking ratios, premises, safeguarding, records and staff suitability. Requirements differ by country and change, so read current guidance and keep evidence of compliance ready.

keyPoints: Leadership sets direction and culture; management runs staffing, money, records and compliance.
Adult-to-child ratios are legal minimums set by regulators and vary by country and age.
Supervision is regular, recorded line management, not just informal help.
A budget balances income against costs and should plan a surplus for reserves.
Keep accurate, secure and confidential records, including attendance, accidents, medication and finances.
Work with parents as partners and keep evidence ready for regulatory inspection.

en.title: Professional Ethics and Conduct in Early Years
en.short: Ethical duties in early years practice, codes of ethics and responding to misconduct.

sections.heading: Ethics and best interests
sections.text: Professional ethics are the standards of right conduct expected in a role. In early years practice, the child’s best interests means putting a child’s safety, wellbeing and development first when decisions are made. It does not mean doing whatever a child wants. A practitioner may need to balance a family’s wishes with the child’s need for rest, play or protection. When safeguarding concerns arise, the child’s safety normally overrides other duties, including confidentiality. Codes of ethics help practitioners reason, but they do not replace law, employer policy or professional judgement.

sections.heading: Codes compared
sections.text: The NAEYC Code of Ethical Conduct (United States) sets out core values, ideals and principles, with responsibilities to children, families, colleagues and community. Its principle that practitioners shall not harm children takes precedence over all others. The Early Childhood Australia Code of Ethics uses core principles and commitments to action, with strong emphasis on social justice, inclusion and cultural responsiveness. Both require confidentiality, respectful partnerships with families and fair treatment. They differ in structure and emphasis, so read the code that governs your setting and note that legal duties vary by country.

sections.heading: Confidentiality and fairness
sections.text: Confidentiality means keeping personal information private. Share it only with those who need it, and usually with consent, unless a child is at risk. Respectful relationships with families involve listening, explaining decisions, avoiding blame and learning about the family’s culture. Fairness means treating children equitably, challenging bias and applying rules consistently, while making reasonable adjustments for disability or language needs.

sections.heading: Responding to misconduct
sections.text: Unethical practice must not be ignored. In a nursery in Ibadan, Nigeria, Ada sees a colleague post a child’s photo on a personal social media account without consent. If a child is in immediate danger, intervene. Otherwise record facts, not opinions, and report promptly to the manager or designated safeguarding lead under setting policy. If the concern is not addressed, escalate to the owner or the relevant regulator. Whistleblowing protections vary by country, so check local law before acting.

keyPoints: Professional ethics are the standards of right conduct expected in a role.
The child’s best interests puts safety, wellbeing and development first.
Confidentiality limits sharing, but safeguarding can override it.
NAEYC and Early Childhood Australia codes share child-centred values but differ in structure.
Fairness means consistent, equitable treatment and challenging bias.
Report unethical practice through policy and escalate if needed; protections vary by country.

en.title: Reflective Practice and Action Research
en.short: Reflective journals, small-scale action research and ethical research with children and staff.

sections.heading: Reflective practice
sections.text: Reflective practice means thinking carefully about your own work to improve it. Reflection on action happens after an event; reflection in action happens while you work. Ask what happened, why, what you would keep and what you would change. Use evidence from observation and children’s responses rather than blame. The aim is professional learning, not proving yourself right.

sections.heading: Keeping a journal
sections.text: Keeping a journal means writing regular, short entries. Record the date, context, what was said and done, your feelings, questions and next steps. Separate facts from interpretations. Write soon after the event, because memory fades. Do not put children’s full names or identifying details in an insecure notebook; store it securely and follow your setting’s policy. Read old entries to spot patterns for action research.

sections.heading: Action research cycle
sections.text: Action research is small-scale, systematic inquiry by a practitioner into their own setting. Identify a narrow problem from your journal or observation. Plan one change with clear success criteria and a timeline. Act, then gather evidence from several sources, such as tallies, notes, children’s work and views from staff or parents. Review for patterns, compare before and after, and ask a colleague to check your interpretation. Share what you learn; the aim is local improvement, not a general law. For example, Mrs Okafor in Enugu noticed few girls used the construction area. She added photos of women builders and invited a parent builder.
