Over ten sessions before, she counted 3 girls; over ten after, 9. She also kept notes and asked a colleague to observe.

sections.heading: Ethics with children and staff
sections.text: Research with children needs ethical care. Seek permission from parents or guardians and assent, the child’s own agreement. Children may refuse or withdraw without penalty. Avoid pressure, keep a familiar adult nearby, and stop if the child seems distressed. Staff consent must be voluntary, with anonymity (no names) and confidentiality (limited sharing) protected; power differences matter. Check setting policy, local law and any ethics committee, store data securely, and report findings fairly.

keyPoints: Reflective practice uses evidence from your own work to decide what to keep and what to change.
A journal separates facts from interpretations and helps you spot patterns.
Action research is a small, systematic cycle: identify a problem, plan a change, act, gather evidence and review.
Use several evidence sources and ask a colleague to check your interpretation.
Research with children requires parent or guardian permission and the child’s assent, and children may withdraw.
Staff consent must be voluntary, and anonymity, confidentiality and secure data handling are essential; check local policy and any required ethics approval.

en.title: Teaching Practice and Field Experience
en.short: Preparing for placement, observing, planning and leading activities, mentoring, portfolios and assessment.

sections.heading: Preparing for placement
sections.text: Teaching practice, also called field experience or practicum, is a supervised period in a real early years setting such as a nursery, preschool or reception class. Before you start, learn the setting’s routines, its safeguarding and behaviour policies, and the age group you will join. Read your handbook and set goals with your tutor. For example, Amina, a student in Kano, reads the safeguarding policy and learns the names of the children in her group before her first day. She writes three goals: to observe transitions, to plan one story activity, and to lead outdoor play.

sections.heading: Observing, planning and leading
sections.text: Observation means watching children closely to understand their interests and needs without interrupting. Keep notes factual and brief. Use what you see to plan activities that match the children’s stage. A plan states the aim, materials, steps and how you will check learning. Start by co-leading with your mentor, then lead short activities. For example, Amina notices the children enjoy sorting stones, so she plans a counting game with local seeds. She keeps the group small and has a backup plan.

sections.heading: Working with a mentor
sections.text: A mentor is an experienced practitioner who guides you in the setting. Agree regular meeting times. Ask for feedback after each activity, and act on it. Keep a portfolio: a folder of plans, observation notes, photos taken with permission, feedback and your own reflections. Reflection means thinking about what went well and what you would change. The portfolio is evidence for assessment.

sections.heading: Assessment against standards
sections.text: You are assessed against professional standards, which are the expected knowledge, skills and values for early years teachers. These differ by country; check your national regulator or awarding body. In Nigeria, the Teachers Registration Council of Nigeria (TRCN) sets teacher standards; in England, early years educator criteria apply. Assessment may include a mentor’s report, a tutor’s visit and a portfolio review. Be honest about mistakes. Standards usually cover safeguarding, planning, relationships with children and families, and professional conduct.

keyPoints: Teaching practice is a supervised placement where you learn to observe, plan and lead activities.
Prepare by reading policies and setting goals with your tutor.
Observe children factually and use your notes to plan suitable activities.
Work closely with your mentor and act on feedback.
Keep a portfolio of plans, observations, feedback and reflections as evidence.
Professional standards differ by country; check your regulator and be honest about mistakes.

en.title: Critical Perspectives on Early Childhood
en.short: Child-centred versus academic debate, children’s rights, developmental norms, sociology and African views.

sections.heading: Child-centred or academic?
sections.text: Child-centred education follows children’s interests and play and treats development holistically. The academic approach, sometimes called didactic, stresses explicit teaching of letters, numbers and school routines. The debate is real but often a false binary: many settings blend guided play with short, planned instruction. Ask what evidence supports each goal, for whom, and at what cost to wellbeing.

sections.heading: Rights-based views
sections.text: A rights-based view sees the child as a holder of rights, not only an object of care. The UN Convention on the Rights of the Child (1989) is widely ratified. Its general principles include non-discrimination, the best interests of the child, survival and development, and respect for the child’s views. Participation means listening to children according to age and maturity. Tensions arise over adult authority, safety and scarce resources.

sections.heading: Norms and sociology
sections.text: Developmental norms are typical ages or milestones drawn from research. Critics note that many early samples were Western and middle-class, so norms can misread culture, language and context and become deficit labels. The sociology of childhood treats childhood as socially constructed and children as social actors. It studies generational order: how power is arranged between adults and children. This does not deny biology; it asks how biology is interpreted.

sections.heading: Postcolonial and African views
sections.text: Postcolonial critique asks whether imported curricula, tests and English-only rules carry colonial assumptions. African perspectives are plural. Many stress communal care, extended family, local language, indigenous play and values such as ubuntu in southern Africa, without claiming one African model. Invented case: in a Kenyan town, Wanjiku’s private preschool advertises reading at four; a community centre favours play in the local language. Parents disagree. A critical response asks whose goals count, what evidence exists, and whether rights and culture are both respected.

keyPoints: Child-centred and academic approaches are often blended; ask about evidence, goals and wellbeing.
Rights-based views treat children as rights holders, with best interests and participation as key principles.
Developmental norms can become deficit labels when culture and context are ignored.
The sociology of childhood sees childhood as socially constructed and children as social actors.
Postcolonial critique questions imported curricula, tests and language rules.
African perspectives are plural; communal care and ubuntu are examples, not a single model.

en.title: Research Methods in Early Childhood
en.short: Designing a dissertation: questions, literature, methods, sampling, ethics with children, analysis and writing.

sections.heading: Designing the study
sections.text: Research design is the plan linking question, methods, sampling and analysis. Start with a focused research question, not a broad topic. Ask what you want to describe, explain or compare. A literature review shows what is already known, identifies the gap, and helps refine the question. For example, a student in Accra might ask: How do four nursery teachers decide when to intervene in children’s disputes? This is narrow for one term.

sections.heading: Methods and sampling
sections.text: Quantitative methods test measurable relationships using numbers, such as questionnaires or structured observation. Qualitative methods explore meaning and experience using interviews, focus groups or field notes. Mixed methods combine both. Sampling is how you choose participants. Probability sampling, such as random selection, supports generalisation. Purposive sampling chooses information-rich cases. Convenience sampling is quick but weak. Justify your sample size and pilot your instruments: interview guide, questionnaire or observation schedule. If 48 of 60 parents return questionnaires, the response rate is 48 ÷ 60 = 80%.

sections.heading: Ethics with children
sections.text: Children are a vulnerable group. Seek ethics committee approval, gatekeeper permission and informed consent from parents or guardians. Children also give assent in language they understand, and may refuse or withdraw. Explain the study simply. Protect confidentiality, store data securely, and have a plan if a child discloses harm. Researchers must not promise secrecy that conflicts with safeguarding duties. Avoid power pressure: a teacher-researcher should not recruit their own pupils without safeguards.

sections.heading: Analysis and writing
sections.text: Qualitative data are usually transcribed, coded and grouped into themes; check themes against the data and keep a record of decisions. Quantitative data are cleaned, then summarised with frequencies, means or percentages, and tested with suitable statistics. Do not confuse correlation with cause. Write up the rationale, methods, findings, discussion and limitations. Report negative or unexpected findings. A small case: Amina, in Kano, interviews four teachers purposively, observes twice, codes transcripts, and asks a peer to review her themes. She reports that four teachers is a limitation, not a representative sample.

keyPoints: A dissertation question should be focused, researchable and linked to a gap in the literature.
Quantitative methods measure variables with numbers; qualitative methods explore meaning; mixed methods combine both.
Probability sampling supports generalisation, purposive sampling selects information-rich cases, and sample size must be justified.
Children give assent as well as parent or guardian consent, and safeguarding duties override promises of secrecy.
Qualitative analysis codes data into themes; quantitative analysis summarises and tests data, and correlation is not cause.
Response rate = returned questionnaires ÷ distributed questionnaires × 100; for example, 48 ÷ 60 = 80%.

en.title: Quality and Evaluation in Early Childhood Services
en.short: Defining and measuring quality, structural and process quality, inspection and using evidence to improve.

sections.heading: Defining quality
sections.text: Quality in early childhood services is not one fixed thing. It is a judgement about how well a service supports children’s wellbeing, learning and participation, and it depends on values, culture, policy goals and the age of the children. A useful definition treats quality as multidimensional: safe conditions, responsive relationships, purposeful learning, inclusion, and family partnership. Because it is value-laden, a measure built in one country may not fit another without adaptation.

sections.heading: Structural and process quality
sections.text: Structural quality covers inputs that can be regulated or counted: staff qualifications and training, adult-child ratios, group size, space, equipment, health and safety, and working conditions. Process quality covers what children actually experience: interactions, pedagogy, language, routines, emotional climate and peer relationships. Structural features can enable good process, but they do not guarantee it. A room may meet every ratio rule and still offer weak interaction. Measures therefore combine administrative data, checklists and validated observation tools, used by trained observers.

sections.heading: Evaluation and inspection
sections.text: Evaluation is the systematic judging of a service against agreed criteria. Inspection is a regulatory form of evaluation, usually checking compliance and sometimes overall quality. Countries use different frameworks: inspection, accreditation, and quality rating and improvement systems that combine ratings with support. England’s Ofsted inspects early years providers, for example, but its framework is national and changes; readers should check their own current official source. Good frameworks use published criteria, trained evaluators, moderation and appeals.

sections.heading: Evidence into practice
sections.text: Evidence should improve practice, not just label settings. Use several sources: self-evaluation, observation, staff and family views, records. Triangulate, meaning compare sources before deciding. Then plan a small change, monitor it, and review. A setting rates three domains 3, 4 and 5 out of 5. The mean is (3 + 4 + 5) ÷ 3 = 12 ÷ 3 = 4.0. The mean hides the weak domain, so read the profile and act on the 3. Check that tools are culturally valid and do not reduce quality to one score.

keyPoints: Quality in early childhood is multidimensional and value-laden, so no single measure is universal.
Structural quality covers countable inputs such as ratios, group size, staff qualifications and space.
Process quality covers children’s actual experiences, especially interactions, pedagogy and emotional climate.
Evaluation judges services against criteria; inspection is regulatory evaluation and frameworks differ by country.
Use multiple valid sources and triangulation before judging quality.
A mean can hide a weak domain, so read the profile and act on specific scores.

en.title: Comparative and International Early Childhood Policy
en.short: Comparing access, equity, financing and workforce across countries, and lessons for policy transfer.

sections.heading: Framing comparison
sections.text: Comparative policy asks how countries organise early childhood education and care (ECEC), meaning services for young children before primary school. Pre-primary education is the organised part. Ages, definitions and providers differ, so compare like with like. Use the UNESCO Institute for Statistics, the Global Education Monitoring Report, OECD Education at a Glance and national plans. Check each figure’s year and definition.

sections.heading: Access and equity
sections.text: Access means whether a child can attend; it is measured by enrolment, attendance and legal entitlement. Many European systems fund public places; many Asian systems mix public provision with private markets; many African systems rely on community, faith and private providers with uneven regulation. These are broad patterns, not rules. Equity means all children can benefit, with extra support for poverty, disability, rural isolation and language barriers.

sections.heading: Financing and workforce
sections.text: Financing covers public spending, household fees, aid and social protection. Compare the share of gross domestic product (GDP) spent on pre-primary, not only total education spending. Suppose education gets 4% of GDP and one quarter goes to pre-primary: 4% × 0.25 = 1% of GDP. This example is invented. Workforce policy covers qualifications, pay, ratios and training. Low pay and poor conditions weaken quality, especially where staff are mainly women.

sections.heading: Policy transfer
sections.text: Policy transfer means using ideas from another country, by voluntary borrowing or by conditions attached to loans. It rarely works as a direct copy. Ask whether the receiving country has the money, teachers and data to sustain it, and whether local families and languages fit. Pilot first, evaluate honestly, and adapt. Donor pressure and rankings can push countries to adopt models that do not fit their context.

keyPoints: Comparative policy compares ECEC systems using official data such as UIS, GEM Report and OECD sources.
Definitions, ages and providers differ between countries, so compare like with like.
Access is measured by enrolment, attendance and legal entitlement; equity adds fairness and inclusion.
Compare pre-primary spending as a share of GDP or budget, not only total education spending.
Workforce qualifications, pay, ratios and conditions shape quality.
Policy transfer needs money, staff, data and local adaptation, not direct copying.
